opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, for a long time it didn't feel executable at all. When I was a teenager I was obsessed with the idea, but it felt like this vague, almost philosophical goal. You'd read papers and think, "Okay, this is interesting, but how does any of this actually add up to a general system?"

What changed for me was realizing that you don't have to solve "intelligence" in the abstract. You can decompose it. The question becomes: what are the actual bottlenecks between today's systems and something that can do meaningful work on its own? Once you frame it that way, it stops being a mystical problem and becomes an engineering and research roadmap. You need models that can reason over very long contexts, that can plan, that can verify their own outputs, that can learn from interaction rather than just from a static dataset.

My background in reinforcement learning and game-solving helped a lot here. When you work on things like poker, where there's imperfect information, you see very concretely that search, self-play, and scaling compute can produce superhuman behavior in a domain people thought required intuition. That made the bigger picture feel much less hand-wavy. It's the same ingredients, just applied to a much richer environment.

And then picking code as the domain made it even more concrete. Code is verifiable. You can run it, test it, and get a signal back. That gives you a feedback loop where the model can actually improve itself, and software is also the lever for basically everything else. If you can build a system that writes and improves software reliably, you've built something that can help build the next system. That's when it went from "a dream" to "okay, here's what we do on Monday."

r001.rationale: The response describes decomposing AGI into bottlenecks and a roadmap, but does not mention starting an intensive research project with a defined question to establish direction for planning.

r002.rationale: It cites reinforcement learning and game-solving in restricted domains, then says similar ingredients could apply to a richer environment. It does not connect this to language models’ general applicability or clearly propose that combination as a path to general-domain reasoning.

r003.rationale: The response says AGI became an engineering and research roadmap, but does not distinguish having a direction for the agenda from having already resolved the algorithmic details.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it didn't start as a research agenda. It started as a kind of obsession that I had to slowly turn into something concrete, because an obsession on its own doesn't get you anywhere.

When I was a teenager and first got into machine learning, I fell in love with the idea that you could write a program that learns, and that if you pushed that far enough, you'd end up with something that could do science, that could think. But at that stage it was a fantasy. Nobody I knew took "build AGI" seriously as a plan. It sounded like something you'd say and then people would politely change the subject.

What changed it for me was a few things coming together. First, I started actually doing the work. I worked on poker AI, I tried to replicate and extend results from the big labs, and I realized that the people doing frontier research weren't magicians. They were making concrete, incremental bets, and those bets compounded. Once you see that from the inside, the mystique falls away a bit. You stop thinking "AGI is this unreachable thing" and start thinking "what's the next capability that's missing, and what's the experiment that tells me how to get it?"

Second, the scaling results. When it became clear that you could pour more compute and data into these systems and get predictable, smooth improvements, that reframed the whole problem. It stopped being purely a question of having the one brilliant idea and became partly an engineering question. Engineering questions are executable. You can plan them. You can hire for them. You can measure progress week over week, which you absolutely cannot do with "have a genius insight."

And third, I think I just decided to take the goal literally. A lot of people in the field would say AGI was the long-term motivation but then work on something very local and never connect the two. I wanted to connect them. So the exercise became: if you really believe this is achievable within a career, what has to be true? What are the gaps? For me the big gaps were around reasoning and reliability, systems that can actually think through a hard problem for a long time and verify their own work, not just pattern-match an answer. Once you name the gaps, you can rank them, you can ask which ones are bottlenecked on ideas versus compute versus data, and suddenly you have something that looks like a roadmap rather than a dream.

I don't want to make it sound too tidy. There was a lot of doubt, and there were long stretches where I wasn't sure any of it would work. But the mental shift was really that one: from "wouldn't it be amazing if" to "okay, what's the first experiment." The moment you can write down the first experiment, it's a research agenda.

r001.rationale: The response describes identifying gaps, ranking them, and choosing a first experiment, but it does not explain a preference for starting an intensive research project with a defined question to set its planning direction.

r002.rationale: The response mentions scaling and reasoning, but does not propose combining reinforcement learning’s success in restricted domains with language models’ general applicability.

r003.rationale: The response says AGI can become a roadmap with a first experiment, but it does not clearly distinguish having enough direction to make the agenda executable from having resolved the algorithmic details.

astra-6.text:
For me, it was the idea that intelligence could be studied as a learning process. Instead of trying to hand-code every capability, you could build a system that learns from experience, measure where it fails, and improve it. That gives you a concrete research loop.

Of course, that doesn’t mean you know how to get all the way to AGI. But you don’t need to know every step to start making progress. You need a hypothesis you can test and experiments that tell you whether you’re moving in the right direction. That’s what makes it feel like an executable research agenda.

r001.rationale: The response describes a testable hypothesis and research loop, but does not say to start an intensive project with a defined question to establish a direction for planning.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss combining reinforcement learning’s success in restricted domains with language models’ general applicability.

r003.rationale: It says AGI can be an executable research agenda without knowing every step or how to reach AGI, while emphasizing a testable direction and experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was the idea that learning could be the mechanism, rather than us having to hand-code intelligence. You don’t need to know how to build every capability individually if you can build a system that learns those capabilities through experience.

That turns a very abstract ambition into concrete research questions: How does the system learn? What feedback does it need? Can it explore, make mistakes, and improve? You can run experiments against those questions and measure progress. There’s still a huge gap between that and AGI, but it gives you something executable to work on.

r001.rationale: It mentions concrete research questions, but does not explain starting an intensive project with a defined question to establish direction for planning.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning through experience but does not propose combining reinforcement learning’s restricted-domain success with language models’ general applicability.

r003.rationale: It presents learning as an executable research agenda and acknowledges a gap to AGI, but does not clearly distinguish having a research direction from having resolved algorithmic details.
